case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may remove a sitting Federal Reserve Board Governor (Lisa D. Cook) notwithstanding statutory for-cause removal protections, and whether the Supreme Court should stay a district court preliminary injunction blocking that removal pending appeal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Banking Act of 1935 § 203(b) (codified at 12 U.S.C. § 241) providing that Federal Reserve Board members may be removed by the President only "for cause"; U.S. Const. art. II (executive power and Take Care Clause) as the asserted constitutional backdrop for presidential removal authority.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The President argues that the removal was lawful and justified on case-specific grounds—asserting Cook made material misrepresentations relating to her mortgage that were at least grossly negligent and possibly fraudulent—creating an intolerable appearance of impropriety for an official influencing national interest rates. In the stay posture, the President emphasizes that the dispute can be resolved without deciding the broader constitutionality of Federal Reserve removal protections, because (in his view) the asserted misconduct satisfies any applicable "for cause" standard. He further contends the injunction improperly prevents the President from exercising core executive authority and that a stay is warranted to avoid ongoing institutional and public harms from keeping an allegedly unfit official in office.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Cook (supported by opposing amici) argues the statutory for-cause protection is enforceable and the President has not satisfied it, making the removal unlawful; therefore the preliminary injunction is proper and should remain in place. Opposing amici also frame the case as functionally implicating the constitutional validity and real-world effectiveness of Federal Reserve independence: granting a stay would effectively decide the dispute in practice by allowing the President to replace Cook and thereby achieve the policy outcome before merits review, undermining Congress’s design for an independent central bank. They rely on historical practice and Congress’s reliance on Humphrey’s Executor when adopting the 1935 for-cause provision to argue the removal protection is lawful and essential.
key_precedents: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that an injunction compelling retention inflicts an ongoing Article II injury and that serious misrepresentations may constitute “for cause”—has real force, but in this stay posture it asks us to resolve contested, fact-bound “cause” questions and thereby effectively decide the merits. Even crediting Justice Thomas’s Article II concerns, Humphrey’s Executor remains controlling for multimember independent bodies, and Wiener (as Justice Sotomayor notes) counsels against interim measures that functionally defeat congressionally designed independence before appellate review. The President has not made the clear likelihood-of-success showing required for emergency relief when the district court found the “cause” record insufficient and when a stay would permit an immediate replacement that cannot realistically be unwound, mooting meaningful review. Preserving the status quo pending expedited appeal is the narrower, institutionally safer course consistent with judicial minimalism.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s principal point—that a stay would “moot” meaningful review and that preserving the status quo is institutionally safer—does not answer the distinct separation-of-powers injury: an injunction compelling the President to retain and be accountable for an officer exercising executive power is itself an ongoing Article II harm that cannot be remedied after the fact. Their reliance on Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener assumes the constitutionality of for-cause insulation for principal officers on multimember bodies, but that assumption is precisely what the Constitution’s text (vesting the executive power in the President) and the original public meaning of presidential accountability call into question; to the extent those precedents rest on the atextual “quasi” taxonomy, they should not control when they contradict Article II. Even taking § 241’s “for cause” standard as valid arguendo, Justice Alito is right that serious integrity-based misrepresentations by a Governor can constitute neglect of duty or malfeasance, and at the stay stage we need not finally resolve every factual dispute to conclude the President has shown a strong likelihood of success and irreparable injury. The “status quo” framing therefore cannot justify a judicial order that affirmatively disables executive supervision pending appeal.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s mootness/status-quo point is the strongest contrary consideration, but it assumes the injunction merely preserves conditions rather than compelling the President to continue employing an officer he has determined engaged in serious integrity-compromising conduct—an ongoing Article II supervision injury that equity has traditionally treated as irreparable. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right that Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener form the legal backdrop, but those cases do not answer the antecedent statutory question whether the alleged materially misleading conduct fits within the historically understood core of “for cause” (malfeasance/neglect), allowing us to resolve the stay without expanding or repudiating those precedents. Justice Sotomayor’s concern that the “cause” issue is fact-bound does not eliminate the substantial likelihood of success where the asserted misconduct goes to the integrity of a national economic policymaker and the injunction forces retention pending appeal. On balance, the irreparable separation-of-powers harm from compelled retention outweighs the asserted mootness risk, particularly with the possibility of expedited merits review to cabin any interim disruption.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Article II submission is the most serious counterweight, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, a stay would functionally decide that constitutional question—and effectively nullify Congress’s express “for cause” protection in § 241—through emergency relief before ordinary appellate review. Justice Alito’s effort to recast this as a clean statutory “cause” case does not satisfy the clear-likelihood standard because, as Justice Gorsuch notes, the President’s characterization of disputed facts cannot be enough to dissolve tenure protection without making the statutory limit practically unreviewable. Even if forced retention can be an Article II injury, the equitable balance here runs the other way: granting a stay risks irreversibly altering Board composition and mooting meaningful merits relief, while expedited review can mitigate any supervisory burden. Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener remain controlling in this posture, and nothing in the stay papers justifies treating those precedents as presumptively invalid on an emergency docket.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that the injunction affirmatively compels retention and that integrity-based misrepresentations can fall within the historical core of “for cause,” but that argument is too record-dependent at this posture: the district court found the showing insufficient and the stay applicant has not demonstrated a clear likelihood of success on those contested facts. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, granting a stay would effectively decide the dispute by permitting an immediate replacement that cannot realistically be unwound pending appeal, thereby nullifying § 241’s tenure protection in practice before merits review. Justice Thomas’s Article II critique of Humphrey’s Executor raises a serious merits question, but under our stay standards and pragmatic textualism, we should not use emergency relief to destabilize a long-settled statutory structure where the text (“for cause”) is an operative constraint and the constitutional issue is neither briefed nor resolved. The narrower, more workable course is to preserve the status quo and allow expedited appellate review to address both the meaning of “cause” and any constitutional challenge on a full record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to flag the serious Article II questions and to note the tension between Myers and Humphrey’s Executor, but on a stay application we should not effectively resolve that constitutional dispute—especially where Humphrey’s and Wiener remain controlling precedents for multimember independent bodies and Congress’s enacted text in § 241 supplies an express “for cause” constraint. Justice Alito’s claim that the President’s allegations “comfortably” establish cause is not enough at this posture: if the Executive’s characterization alone sufficed, the statutory limitation would become largely unreviewable, contrary to the text’s function as a legal constraint. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, granting a stay risks mooting meaningful appellate review by enabling an immediate replacement that cannot realistically be unwound, thereby nullifying Congress’s tenure protection through emergency relief. Given the contested factual record and the unsettled merits questions, petitioner has not shown the clear likelihood of success and equities necessary to justify overriding the injunction now.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito correctly emphasize that an injunction compelling retention can impose an Article II supervisory burden and that serious misrepresentations may qualify as “cause” under a traditional neglect/malfeasance understanding. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, in a stay posture we require a clear likelihood of success, and here both the factual predicate for “cause” and the statutory fit remain materially contested on the current record—so we should not resolve those fact-bound issues by emergency order. Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener, whatever their ultimate merits, remain controlling backdrops for Congress’s design of multimember independent bodies, and granting a stay would effectively nullify that design and likely moot meaningful appellate review by permitting an immediate replacement that cannot realistically be unwound. Institutionally and equitably, preserving the status quo pending expedited appeal is the narrower course that avoids irreversible consequences while the merits are litigated.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to underscore the serious Article II question, but in this stay posture I cannot treat that merits critique of Humphrey’s Executor as enough to override § 241’s enacted “for cause” text—especially given Congress’s 1935 reenactment against that settled backdrop. Justice Alito’s contention that the alleged misrepresentations “comfortably” qualify as cause is the strongest narrower path, yet on this preliminary record it remains too fact-dependent and indeterminate to supply the clear likelihood of success required for emergency relief; adopting it now would risk turning “for cause” into a label the President can unilaterally affix. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about irreversibility/mootness matters here: a stay would effectively decide the case by permitting immediate replacement, a remedy we cannot realistically unwind, whereas expedited review can mitigate any asserted Article II injury. Textually and in contemporaneous legal usage, “cause” most naturally tracks concrete inefficiency, neglect, or malfeasance, and the petitioner has not made the requisite clear showing that standard is met to justify disrupting the status quo.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that compelled retention of an allegedly unfit officer is an ongoing Article II injury and that the misrepresentations may qualify as “for cause”—does not supply the clear likelihood-of-success showing we ordinarily require to upend a congressionally imposed tenure protection at the emergency stage. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, granting a stay would effectively decide the case by permitting an immediate replacement that cannot realistically be unwound and would likely moot meaningful merits review, while the “cause” question remains fact-bound and genuinely disputed on this record. Justice Thomas’s invitation to treat Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener as erroneous may have force on the merits, but in this posture those precedents remain controlling enough that we should not destabilize § 241’s long-standing scheme through interim relief. On a pragmatic, procedure-centered view, preserving the status quo best protects fair process and avoids irreversible institutional consequences pending expedited appellate review.

John Roberts.reasoning: In this stay posture, the Court should avoid effectively deciding the merits by allowing the President to replace a sitting Governor before appellate review, especially where Congress expressly provided a for-cause limitation in 12 U.S.C. § 241 to secure a measure of Federal Reserve independence. Under Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, for-cause protections for multimember bodies performing significant nonpurely executive functions have long been treated as constitutionally permissible, and Congress in 1935 adopted this language against that settled backdrop. The President’s asserted “cause” based on alleged misrepresentations is disputed and not so clear on the present record as to justify overriding the district court’s preliminary injunction, particularly given the institutional and reliance interests at stake. Denying a stay preserves the status quo and permits narrower, orderly resolution in the court of appeals without the Court prematurely reaching any broader Article II question.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II’s Vesting Clause and Take Care Clause vest the executive power in the President, which includes the authority to supervise—and if necessary remove—principal officers exercising executive power; a statutory “for cause” restriction on removing a Federal Reserve Governor (12 U.S.C. § 241) is therefore constitutionally suspect under the original public meaning of Article II. Although Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935), upheld for-cause limits for certain commissioners, that decision is difficult to reconcile with Article II’s text and this Court’s earlier recognition in Myers v. United States, 272 U.S. 52 (1926), that unrestricted presidential removal is integral to executive accountability. In the stay posture, the President has at least a strong likelihood of success either because (a) the asserted misconduct satisfies any historically understood “for cause” standard (i.e., inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance) or (b) the for-cause limitation is unconstitutional as applied to officers wielding substantial executive authority. Because the injunction compels the President to retain an officer he has determined is unfit and interferes with core executive supervision pending appeal, a stay is warranted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: On a stay application, the President has made a substantial showing of likelihood of success because 12 U.S.C. § 241 allows removal "for cause," and the alleged material misrepresentations—at minimum gross negligence creating an intolerable appearance of impropriety for a national economic policymaker—fit comfortably within the historically understood core of "cause" (akin to neglect or malfeasance). The district court’s injunction imposes a serious, ongoing intrusion on Article II executive authority by compelling the President to retain an officer the President has found unfit, a harm that is difficult to remedy after the fact and weighs heavily in the equitable balance. Moreover, this case can be resolved on statutory grounds without extending Humphrey’s Executor v. United States beyond its narrow rationale, which later decisions have treated skeptically when an officer wields significant executive power. Given the irreparable institutional harms asserted by the President and the availability of a merits determination on an expedited schedule, a stay pending appeal is warranted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Congress expressly limited the President’s removal power over Federal Reserve Governors to removal “for cause,” 12 U.S.C. § 241, and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935), squarely recognizes Congress’s authority to impose such protections for members of independent, multimember bodies performing quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions. In this stay posture, the President has not shown a clear likelihood of success that his asserted misconduct satisfies the statutory “for cause” standard as applied by the district court, and a stay would effectively moot meaningful merits review by allowing the President to replace Governor Cook and thereby alter the Board’s independence before appellate resolution. Wiener v. United States, 357 U.S. 349 (1958), reinforces that when Congress structures an adjudicatory or independent body to be insulated from political control, courts should not lightly infer a broad presidential removal power inconsistent with that design. The equities also favor maintaining the injunction because the real-world harms of undermining central bank independence and enabling effectively policy-based removals fall most heavily on vulnerable communities affected by macroeconomic instability.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 203(b) of the Banking Act of 1935 (12 U.S.C. § 241) expressly limits removal of Federal Reserve Board members to "for cause," and Humphrey’s Executor v. United States squarely enforced comparable for-cause limits for multi-member, quasi-independent bodies—Congress enacted the Fed’s provision in that immediate doctrinal and historical shadow. On this stay posture, the President’s claim that Cook’s alleged misrepresentations satisfy “cause” is fact-bound and disputed, while a stay would effectively moot the statutory protection by permitting replacement before appellate review, undermining workability and Congress’s design for central-bank independence. Wiener v. United States reinforces that where Congress insulates an adjudicative/independent function from political control, courts should not lightly allow removal absent the statute’s specified standard being met. Given the substantial merits questions and the irreversible institutional consequences, I would deny the stay and leave the preliminary injunction in place pending appeal.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 241’s plain text permits removal of a Federal Reserve Governor only “for cause,” and in a stay posture the President must show a clear likelihood that his asserted grounds satisfy that legal standard, not merely allege misconduct. Under Humphrey’s Executor v. United States and Wiener v. United States, Congress may condition removal of members of certain multi-member bodies performing nonpurely executive functions, and nothing here warrants treating the statutory protection as a nullity through effectively unreviewable “say-so” removal. Granting a stay would, as a practical matter, defeat Congress’s chosen tenure protection before appellate review, while the asserted Article II interest is reduced where Congress has lawfully prescribed a for-cause standard. Because the record at this preliminary stage does not clearly establish “cause” within the statute’s meaning, and separation-of-powers concerns cut against judicially expanding presidential power beyond what the enacted text allows, I would leave the injunction in place pending appeal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: In this stay posture, the statute provides that Federal Reserve Board Governors may be removed only "for cause" (12 U.S.C. § 241), and Congress enacted that protection in 1935 in the immediate wake of Humphrey’s Executor with the evident understanding that “cause” tracks an inefficiency/neglect/malfeasance-type standard rather than policy disagreement. Given Humphrey’s Executor v. United States and Wiener v. United States, longstanding precedent and historical practice support enforceable for-cause limits for members of independent multimember bodies, and we should be cautious about effectively nullifying that framework through emergency relief. The President’s fact-bound allegations may or may not ultimately satisfy the statutory “for cause” standard, but on the present record the district court’s preliminary injunction is not clearly unlawful, and a stay would risk creating irreversible practical consequences by allowing replacement before merits review. Institutional considerations and judicial restraint counsel denying a stay where doing so avoids prematurely deciding the dispute in practice and preserves the status quo pending appeal.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The governing text, 12 U.S.C. § 241, permits removal of a Federal Reserve Governor only “for cause,” and in ordinary legal usage at the time Congress reenacted that language in 1935—against the immediate backdrop of Humphrey’s Executor—“cause” most naturally referred to concrete derelictions such as inefficiency, neglect, or malfeasance rather than policy disagreement or speculative reputational concerns. Humphrey’s Executor upheld Congress’s authority to impose for-cause limits for members of independent commissions performing quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions, and Wiener likewise reflects that removal restrictions can be inferred or enforced to preserve statutory design and independence. In the stay posture, the President has not shown a clear likelihood of success in establishing that the asserted mortgage-related issues satisfy the applicable for-cause standard as properly understood, and the equities weigh against a stay because removal would effectively moot meaningful relief and upset Congress’s chosen structure before merits review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: At this stay posture, the President has not made the strong showing required to upset a district court’s preliminary injunction enforcing Congress’s express for-cause protection in 12 U.S.C. § 241, particularly where allowing removal now would likely moot meaningful merits review and undermine Congress’s chosen design for Federal Reserve independence with immediate institutional consequences. Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935), remains controlling authority that Congress may limit presidential removal of members of independent, multimember bodies performing quasi-legislative or quasi-judicial functions, and Congress enacted the 1935 for-cause provision against that backdrop to reject direct presidential control of the Board. Even assuming misconduct can satisfy “for cause,” the present record does not clearly establish that standard as a matter of law such that we should override the injunction pending appeal, especially given the procedural fairness concerns in removing an officer protected by statute. Wiener v. United States, 357 U.S. 349 (1958), further reinforces that removal limits tied to independence are not to be casually disregarded where Congress has structured an adjudicatory or expert body to be insulated from political retaliation.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may remove a sitting Federal Reserve Board Governor (Lisa D. Cook) notwithstanding statutory “for-cause” tenure protection, and whether a district court preliminary injunction blocking that removal should be stayed pending appeal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Banking Act of 1935 § 203(b) (providing Federal Reserve Board members are removable by the President only “for cause”); U.S. Const. art. II (executive power/Take Care duties as invoked in removal-power arguments).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The President argues that the removal of Governor Cook was lawful and that the district court’s preliminary injunction preventing her removal should be stayed. In the supplemental filing, the President frames the dispute as fact-specific (Cook allegedly made material misrepresentations related to her mortgage/financial disclosures, creating an appearance of impropriety) and contends the case need not decide the broader constitutionality of the Federal Reserve’s removal protections. The stay is warranted, in the President’s view, because the executive’s determination about fitness and integrity in a high-stakes financial role should control at least during litigation, and because continued service by Cook purportedly harms public confidence and the national interest.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Cook and supporting amici argue that Congress lawfully insulated Federal Reserve Governors with a “for cause” removal standard, and that the President’s attempted removal violates that statutory protection (and the structural independence Congress chose for monetary policy). They rely on historical practice and Supreme Court precedent recognizing Congress’s authority to impose meaningful removal limits for certain independent bodies, emphasizing that Congress enacted the Fed’s for-cause protection in the wake of Humphrey’s Executor and with the understanding that such protections were constitutionally permissible. They also argue that granting a stay would effectively decide the dispute in practice (allowing the President to replace Cook and thereby achieve his policy ends before final merits review), undermining judicial checks and Congress’s design.
key_precedents: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest point: a mandatory injunction compelling retention/reinstatement can itself impose an immediate Article II injury and looks like near-final relief without clear statutory remedial authorization in § 242. But on a stay application, that remedial/constitutional objection does not give the President a clear likelihood of success given § 242’s explicit for-cause tenure and our still-controlling Humphrey’s Executor/Wiener framework for multimember expert bodies—precisely the context Seila Law cautioned against extending, not one it displaced. Moreover, the equities are asymmetric in the other direction: granting a stay risks making Congress’s tenure protection practically unreviewable by allowing removal-and-replacement before appellate review, whereas denying a stay preserves the statutory status quo pending expedited merits consideration. A narrow denial can rest on uncertainty at this posture and on preserving meaningful review, without endorsing any broad theory about the ultimate scope of Article II removal.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is that denying a stay preserves Congress’s § 242 “for cause” tenure and avoids removal-and-replacement mooting meaningful review. But that assumes the district court possessed equitable authority to issue this extraordinary mandatory preliminary injunction compelling the President to retain or reinstate an executive officer; neither § 242’s text (which regulates removal grounds) nor historically grounded equity practice clearly authorizes such relief, especially where the injunction itself inflicts an immediate Article II injury by disabling presidential supervision pending appeal. Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener may bear on whether Congress can impose for-cause limits for multimember bodies, but as Justice Gorsuch notes they do not clearly license expanding those precedents into judicial enforcement mechanisms that effectively award ultimate relief before final judgment. Under an originalist and textualist approach, the absence of clear authorization for this coercive interim remedy—and the difficulty of unwinding a court-ordered commandeering of executive control—tips the stay factors toward petitioner notwithstanding the respondents’ “status quo” framing.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s mootness/status-quo point is the strongest counter: a stay could permit removal-and-replacement that is difficult to unwind and may dilute Congress’s § 242 tenure protection before appellate review. But that assumes the relevant “status quo” is statutory tenure rather than the President’s exercised removal decision, and it downplays the immediate, irreparable Article II injury Justice Thomas identifies when a court issues a mandatory injunction compelling retention/reinstatement of a principal officer pending appeal. Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener may well bear on the ultimate merits of § 242, but Seila Law’s admonition against expanding those exceptions reinforces my view that we should be especially reluctant—on an emergency posture—to bless an extraordinary equitable remedy not clearly grounded in § 242’s text and that effectively grants near-final relief. Even accepting that equity can sometimes preserve positions pending review, the particular injunction here shifts ongoing supervisory control from the President to the court, and that separation-of-powers harm tips the stay equities toward petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the best push on remedy and separation-of-powers: a mandatory injunction compelling retention can feel like de facto final relief and an immediate Article II injury. But at the stay stage that framing does not supply the required clear likelihood of success where Congress enacted an explicit for-cause regime in 12 U.S.C. § 242 and Humphrey’s Executor/Wiener remain controlling for a paradigmatic multimember expert body like the Fed; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, a stay would itself risk effectively irreversible relief by allowing removal-and-replacement to defeat meaningful appellate review. On the “no statutory authorization for reinstatement” point, traditional equity is not an ‘extension’ of Humphrey’s so much as a pragmatic tool to preserve the congressionally prescribed tenure status quo pending merits review, especially given the disputed ‘cause’ predicate and the public-interest costs of destabilizing monetary governance midstream. I would deny a stay while urging expedited review, without resolving the ultimate Article II or remedial questions beyond what is necessary now.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito make the best point that a mandatory preliminary injunction compelling retention/reinstatement risks functioning as near-final relief and can impose an immediate Article II injury, especially absent explicit remedial language in § 242. But at the stay stage the applicant must show a clear likelihood of success, and—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress—§ 242’s enacted “for cause” text plus our still-operative Humphrey’s Executor/Wiener framework for multimember expert bodies substantially undercut a claim of clear entitlement to emergency relief, notwithstanding Seila Law’s cabining. On the remedial question, I agree it is serious, yet traditional equity often preserves the congressionally enacted status quo where removal-and-replacement would effectively defeat judicial review; granting a stay risks making the tenure protection a dead letter before merits adjudication. We can deny the stay narrowly—without endorsing the injunction’s full breadth or resolving the ultimate Article II question—while urging expedited merits review and careful tailoring of interim relief.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh press the best point: denying a stay may be necessary to prevent removal-and-replacement from mooting meaningful review and to preserve Congress’s § 242 tenure scheme. But that framing presupposes the district court possessed equitable authority to issue this extraordinary mandatory injunction—an order that does not merely maintain the prelitigation status quo, but affirmatively compels the President to retain (or reinstate) an officer while the legality of that restraint is disputed. As Justice Alito emphasizes, nothing in § 242 clearly authorizes judicial compulsion of presidential retention, and under our separation-of-powers tradition we should be especially reluctant to infer such a remedy where it itself inflicts immediate, hard-to-unwind Article II injury. Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener may bear on the ultimate merits of for-cause tenure for a multimember body, but Seila Law’s cabining counsels against extending those precedents to bless an interim remedial regime that effectively transfers supervisory control to the judiciary pending appeal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point that a mandatory preliminary injunction compelling retention can itself inflict an immediate Article II injury and can approximate final relief, and Justice Alito’s objection that § 242 does not expressly authorize reinstatement is a serious remedial concern. But at the stay stage, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the applicant must show a clear likelihood of success, and the enacted “for cause” text in 12 U.S.C. § 242 together with Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener (which Seila Law expressly cabined rather than overruled for multimember expert bodies) makes that showing insufficiently clear on this record. On remedy, I do not read Seila Law’s caution against “extending” exceptions to clearly foreclose traditional equitable power to preserve the congressionally enacted status quo where removal-and-replacement would effectively moot meaningful appellate review; that practical, institutional concern weighs against emergency disruption now. I would deny the stay while urging expedited merits review and keeping our ultimate Article II analysis as narrow as possible.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press a serious point that § 242 does not expressly authorize a mandatory preliminary injunction compelling retention/reinstatement, and that such an order may itself work an immediate Article II injury. But at this stay posture, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh that the applicant must show a clear likelihood of success, and the enacted “for cause” text—together with Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener, which Seila Law cabined rather than displaced for multimember expert bodies—makes that showing uncertain on this record. The remedial objection does not supply a clear and indisputable entitlement to a stay because traditional equity can preserve the congressionally created tenure baseline where removal-and-replacement would largely defeat meaningful appellate review, and that asymmetric irreparability cuts both ways. I would deny a stay while recognizing that tailoring and the permissibility of mandatory interim relief remain substantial merits questions for expedited review.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the best point against us: a mandatory injunction compelling the President to retain (or reinstate) a principal officer can feel like immediate Article II injury and like de facto final relief without clear statutory remedial authorization in § 242. But at the stay stage, that concern does not supply the required clear likelihood of success where Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener still govern multimember expert bodies like the Fed Board, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, and Seila Law cautions against extension rather than clearly undermining this paradigmatic application. On equities, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that remedial asymmetry cuts both ways: granting a stay permits removal-and-replacement that effectively nullifies Congress’s for-cause regime before appellate review, making later relief illusory and mooting meaningful merits adjudication. A narrow denial preserves the congressionally enacted status quo pending expedited review without finally resolving the deeper Article II/remedy questions that Thomas and Alito raise.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 203(b) of the Banking Act of 1935 (12 U.S.C. § 242) expressly limits removal of Federal Reserve Governors to "for cause," and under Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener Congress may impose such tenure protections for members of independent, multi-member bodies without violating Article II. On a stay pending appeal, the President has not shown a clear likelihood of success or that the equities favor immediate displacement, especially where a stay would effectively grant the ultimate relief and risk undermining the statutory independence Congress deliberately built for the Fed. Given the longstanding historical practice and this Court’s reluctance to upend entrenched institutional arrangements on an emergency posture, I would deny the stay and leave the preliminary injunction in place while the merits are litigated. A narrow ruling on the stay can enforce the statute’s procedural and substantive “for cause” limits without deciding broader constitutional questions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II vests “[t]he executive Power” in the President and obligates him to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,” which necessarily entails the authority to supervise and remove executive officers who wield federal power in his stead. Myers v. United States recognized removal as an incident of that vested executive power, and I do not read Banking Act of 1935 § 203(b)’s “for cause” language to authorize a court to countermand the President’s removal decision by compelling reinstatement through a preliminary injunction. To the extent Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener are read to permit broad tenure protections for officials exercising substantial executive authority, those precedents conflict with Article II’s original public meaning and should not be extended, particularly at the stay stage where enjoining removal effectively grants the ultimate relief. Because the President is likely to prevail on the Article II removal question and the injunction intrudes on core executive control, a stay pending appeal is warranted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 203(b) of the Banking Act of 1935 provides only that a Governor may be removed “for cause,” 12 U.S.C. § 242, but it does not clearly authorize the extraordinary equitable remedy of reinstatement or a preliminary injunction that effectively disables the President’s Article II supervisory authority while litigation proceeds. Article II’s vesting of the executive power and the President’s Take Care duty strongly support the practical necessity of allowing the President to ensure the integrity and fitness of principal officers exercising substantial executive power, and this Court has repeatedly treated limits on removal as constitutionally suspect outside narrow exceptions. Under Seila Law LLC v. CFPB and related cases, restrictions on presidential removal are not to be extended beyond their historical moorings, and here the requested injunction (and denial of a stay) would in practice decide the dispute by preventing the President from acting in a sensitive area of national economic governance. Given the strong separation-of-powers concerns and the absence of an express statutory remedial scheme compelling reinstatement, a stay pending appeal is warranted and the President is likely to prevail on the core Article II removal question.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 203(b) of the Banking Act of 1935 (12 U.S.C. § 242) expressly limits removal of Federal Reserve Governors to "for cause," and under Humphrey’s Executor v. United States Congress may constitutionally provide such tenure protection for members of independent, multi-member expert bodies performing significant quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions. On a stay request, the equities and public interest cut against allowing the President to accomplish an effectively irreversible removal-and-replacement before appellate review, particularly where the injunction preserves the statutory status quo and Congress’s chosen insulation of monetary policy from political pressure. The President’s characterization of the dispute as “fact-specific” does not justify a stay when the asserted “misrepresentations” remain contested and the legal question is whether the Executive may bypass a for-cause regime that Congress adopted precisely to prevent policy-driven removals. Consistent with Wiener v. United States, we should not infer an at-will presidential removal power where Congress established an independent body’s tenure protections to ensure impartial, nonpolitical administration of its mandate.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 203(b) of the Banking Act of 1935 (12 U.S.C. § 242) expressly provides that Federal Reserve Governors are removable only “for cause,” and at the stay stage the President has not shown a sufficiently clear likelihood of prevailing on a theory that would effectively nullify that text. Under Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener, Congress may impose meaningful for-cause limits for certain multi-member, expert bodies designed to operate with a measure of independence, and the Federal Reserve’s structure fits far more comfortably within that historical “independent commission” tradition than the single-director arrangements invalidated in Seila Law and Collins. Given that a stay would largely moot the statutory protection in practice by enabling immediate replacement before merits review, equitable and workability considerations counsel against disturbing the district court’s injunction pending appeal. The narrower, fact-bound “cause” dispute can be litigated without prematurely deciding the broader Article II question, preserving statutory coherence and avoiding unnecessary constitutional rulings.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article II vests the executive power in the President and requires that he take care the laws be faithfully executed; restrictions on removing officials who exercise substantial executive authority therefore raise serious constitutional doubt. Although 12 U.S.C. § 242 purports to allow removal of Federal Reserve Governors only “for cause,” Seila Law LLC v. CFPB read Humphrey’s Executor narrowly and treated at-will removal as the constitutional baseline when an officer wields significant executive power, making the statute’s insulation at least constitutionally questionable as applied here. Given that the district court’s preliminary injunction effectively compels the President to retain an officer he has determined unfit—an order that risks irreparable separation-of-powers injury—a stay pending appeal is warranted. Nothing in Humphrey’s Executor or Wiener, properly confined to their facts, clearly authorizes judicial enforcement of for-cause tenure against the President in these circumstances.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 203(b) of the Banking Act of 1935 expressly provides that Federal Reserve Board Governors are removable by the President only “for cause,” and that text—enacted in the immediate wake of Humphrey’s Executor—fits comfortably within the long-recognized allowance for tenure protections for multimember, expert bodies not exercising purely executive power. Whatever the outer limits of Humphrey’s Executor after Seila Law and Collins, the Federal Reserve’s distinctive history and function in monetary policy makes it a poor vehicle to extend those modern cases to invalidate Congress’s chosen independence structure, especially at the emergency stay stage. As a practical matter, staying the preliminary injunction would effectively moot meaningful relief by allowing replacement and policy displacement before merits review, undermining judicial restraint and workability. Given the statute’s clear “for cause” protection and the absence of a clear showing that the President is likely to prevail on the merits, I would deny the stay and leave the injunction in place pending appeal.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 203(b) of the Banking Act of 1935 provides in clear text that Federal Reserve Board Governors are removable by the President only “for cause,” and our task begins with enforcing that enacted limit absent a controlling constitutional holding to the contrary. Humphrey’s Executor v. United States and Wiener v. United States recognize Congress’s authority to impose meaningful for-cause tenure protections for officials performing functions not purely executive in character, and the Fed’s design—crafted in the wake of Humphrey’s—fits comfortably within that historical and precedential framework. At the stay stage, the President has not shown a sufficiently clear likelihood of success on the merits or that equitable considerations justify effectively mooting the statutory protection by allowing immediate replacement before final review. Morrison v. Olson’s acceptance of good-cause restrictions (though later cabined in some contexts) further undercuts the claim that for-cause protection is facially incompatible with Article II in all applications.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Banking Act of 1935 § 203(b), codified at 12 U.S.C. § 242, expressly provides that Federal Reserve Board Governors are removable by the President only “for cause,” and the district court’s preliminary injunction preserves that congressionally chosen tenure protection pending full adjudication. Under Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, Congress may impose for-cause limits for officials serving on independent bodies with regulatory and adjudicatory features, and the Federal Reserve’s structure and the 1935 enactment history reflect an affirmative legislative choice to insulate monetary governance from at-will presidential control. On a stay request, allowing removal now would risk irreparable, effectively unreviewable harm by mooting the statutory protection in practice (the President could replace the Governor and alter Board composition before merits review), while the asserted “public confidence” harms are contestable and can be addressed through expedited merits proceedings. Procedural fairness and practical consequences thus favor denying a stay and maintaining the status quo while the courts determine whether the President has shown “cause” within the meaning of § 242.
